items.title: Wycliffe Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001
items.q: Sweets Edison, he was the same way. And if he didn’t like something, he didn’t like it. But he would never be like you need to do this, or these young guys they’re not playing anything.

ctx.x: I’m kind of getting away from the question. But and I think all of that, it has something to do with the way the musicians are towards one another. I think when the bebop era came in and musicians said it’s about me kind of thing, as where there when you were playing music that was more communal like a big band, or when you were playing the New Orleans style or traditional or what they call Dixieland, it was all interactive. It was a

communal thing. It wasn’t about I’m soloing and you know, check out what I’m doing. It was more communal. And I think the guys and ladies, the people that played that music, they were more communal in their approach to life and to each other. And our generation today, because most of the musicians grew up listening to bebop, one thing that I think I dislike is it’s hard sometimes, it seems like a lot of the musicians don’t really get or give props to another musician until after they’re dead and gone. Some of us,…

I think you’re right and I think that some of that comes — some of the lack of that I believes comes from this term I heard recently and that was jazz in the middle ages, that the people that are in that generation of being around 50 or so forth, some of them feel that the younger guys are getting all the marketing support and the record company support and what about me.
